observations.code_quote: - **No author leaderboards or per-developer performance rankings; individual comparison is allowed.** The surveillance risk is turning developer figures into an ordered population or a performance scorecard. It is not an engineer inspecting their own friction, and not a comparison with a colleague they already know. Author figures may therefore be read one author at a time, and compared deliberately with another author, a GitHub team, or the repository. The product must not rank, sort, score or enumerate authors by delivery or CI/PR figures, and a team view must never break its aggregate down into a per-member ranking. The delivery reads (`delivery_summary`, `pull_request_timelines`) take exactly one scope (one author, one GitHub team, or one pull request, defined once in `logic/delivery_scope.py`) and give repository context. `delivery_comparison` gives explicit comparison context: one author's ready-to-merge medians next to the aggregate of the relevant teams and the repository, and next to another author's figures when the person asking named that author. It does not discover, order or return a population of authors. Review pace differs a lot between teams, so the repository median alone cannot say whether an author's wait is normal for the work they do. The read picks the teams from the author's own memberships by one fixed rule, defined once in the logic layer: the teams the pull request in focus asked to review, else the team asked by the most of the author's pull requests, counting each pull request once per team and only requests made in the window, else every team the author is in. Each picked team gets its own row, and teams are never pooled. What a pull request asked comes from its immutable `review_requested` issue events, never from the pull request snapshot, which drops a request once the team reviews. Without those events the rule falls through to every team the author is in. A team scope matches authors through the `team_members` snapshot and matches nothing when it isn't synced. The team page passes its owning team straight through as that scope: an ownership file's team name is already the GitHub org team slug, which `hogli owners:lint --live` validates against the org on every ownership change, so no mapping sits between the two vocabularies. The author page is reached from PR-row author links, and a colleague's page may be opened directly; `author_workflow_costs` and the delivery reads stay UI-only (MCP `enabled: false`).
observations.behavior: Adds explicit guardrails and implementation rules preventing ranked leaderboards while allowing scoped comparisons; this could help PostHog avoid building surveillance features or clarify acceptable use.
observations.posthog_connection: Could support engineering analytics dashboards without introducing ranking-based developer performance tracking, potentially reducing compliance risk and clarifying feature boundaries.

observations.code_quote: - Scope-vs-repository comparison (an author or a team against the repository) renders as `ScopeComparisonCard` ("This author / Repo" bars on one scale). The question there is "is this friction unusual here", which a previous window can't answer. It never renders a ranked, sorted or scrollable list of authors by their figures. The standing extra baseline is the author's own team: the ready-to-merge card draws it as muted rows between the author and the repository, one row per team the comparison picked. Another author joins those rows only when the person asking named that author.
observations.behavior: Defines frontend rendering behavior to prevent leaderboard-style lists and enforce team-baseline comparisons rather than cross-author rankings.
observations.posthog_connection: Provides guidance for implementing an engineering productivity dashboard in PostHog’s frontend, possibly avoiding unintended ranking functionality.
